Images and symptoms are guides only. Similar conditions can look alike. Confirm serious or spreading disease with your municipal or city agriculturist. Use only locally registered crop-protection products and always follow the label.

Black Sigatoka, also known as black leaf streak disease, is one of the most serious fungal diseases affecting banana plants.

It is caused by the fungus Mycosphaerella fijiensis.

This disease attacks the leaves of the banana plant, reducing its ability to perform photosynthesis properly.

As the infection becomes severe, banana production decreases, fruits become smaller, and the overall quality of the harvest is affected.

Black Sigatoka spreads quickly in warm and humid environments, especially during long periods of rainfall.

Panama Disease, also known as Fusarium wilt, is a highly destructive fungal disease caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense.

The fungus attacks the vascular system of the banana plant, blocking the movement of water and nutrients from the roots to the leaves.

This disease is considered one of the most dangerous threats to banana production worldwide because the fungus can survive in the soil for many years.

Once a plantation becomes infected, the disease is very difficult to eliminate completely.

Cordana Leaf Spot is a fungal disease of banana plants caused by Cordana musae.

Although it is generally less destructive than Black Sigatoka, it can still weaken banana plants when left unmanaged.

The disease mainly affects older leaves and is more common in areas with high humidity and poor air circulation.

Continuous infection may reduce photosynthetic activity and affect plant growth and fruit production.

• Dense aggregation of the black streak may form and when these areas become watersoaked, the leaf turns black, dries-up rapidly, and becomes brown
• Small yellowish/chlorotic spots initially appear on the underside of the leaf.
• The spots develop into thin, elongated brown streaks, often running parallel to the leaf veins.
• The streaks gradually become darker brown, reddish-brown, or black.
• Lesions enlarge and develop fusiform or elliptical shapes.
• A yellow/chlorotic halo and sometimes a water-soaked appearance may develop around the lesions.
• Lesions eventually coalesce and form extensive black or brown necrotic areas, resulting in leaf drying and premature leaf death.

Spores move between plants through wind and rain splash. Infection develops fastest during warm, humid weather and long periods of leaf wetness. Dense planting, poor drainage, weeds, and infected leaf material can increase disease pressure.

• Mark affected plants and inspect nearby leaves regularly
• Remove only severely infected or dead leaf tissue with clean tools; do not remove too many functional leaves
• Improve drainage, airflow, weed control, and balanced plant nutrition
• Ask a qualified agriculturist about a local monitoring and fungicide-rotation program; use only products registered for banana and Black Sigatoka

• Start with clean, disease-free planting material
• Keep enough spacing between plants and maintain good field drainage
• Sanitize cutting tools between plants and manage infected leaf debris responsibly
• Check younger leaves frequently, especially during rainy and humid periods
• Avoid repeated use of one fungicide mode of action to reduce resistance risk

• Yellowing of older leaves, usually beginning along the leaf margins and progressing toward the midrib.
• Yellowing and chlorosis progressively spread from older leaves toward younger leaves.
• Affected leaves wilt and collapse at the petiole, causing them to hang around the pseudostem.
• The plant may develop longitudinal splitting at the base of the pseudostem.
• Leaves may become poorly developed or malformed, with normal leaf production eventually declining.
• In severe cases, progressive leaf necrosis, wilting, and plant death occur.

The fungus spreads mainly in infected planting material and contaminated soil carried by water, footwear, tools, machinery, animals, and vehicles. It can remain in infested soil for decades. A plant may be infected for months before obvious symptoms appear.

• Do not uproot, cut, or move a suspected plant, soil, or suckers; this can spread contamination
• Restrict access, mark the area, and contact your municipal or city agriculturist or plant-health authority promptly
• Clean and disinfect footwear, tools, and vehicles before leaving the area under official guidance
• There is no reliable curative fungicide once a plant is infected; containment and expert confirmation are essential

• Use certified disease-free tissue-culture plants or planting material from a trusted source
• Control entry to the farm and keep tools, boots, tires, and equipment free of soil
• Prevent runoff from suspected areas and maintain good drainage
• Never share suckers or soil from an affected field
• Use resistant or tolerant varieties only with advice suited to the local Foc race and production area

• Small black or dark necrotic spots initially appear on the banana leaves.
• The spots enlarge and develop into larger brown necrotic lesions.
• Lesions are commonly surrounded by a yellow/chlorotic halo.
• The center of the lesion becomes light brown to white as it develops.
• Lesions may become oval, elongated, or diamond-shaped, depending on the banana cultivar.
• Severe infection causes lesions to expand and extensive leaf tissue to become necrotic and damaged.

Large numbers of spores form on the underside of lesions and spread during wet, windy weather. The fungus commonly enters through damaged leaf tissue and is more severe on plants stressed by waterlogging, drought, poor nutrition, or weak airflow.

• Remove severely damaged leaf portions using clean, disinfected tools
• Improve drainage, airflow, and balanced nutrition to reduce plant stress
• Check for and manage accompanying Sigatoka leaf spots
• For persistent outbreaks, ask a qualified agriculturist about a locally registered banana leaf-spot program

• Avoid unnecessary leaf injury and keep cutting tools clean
• Remove old, badly affected leaves and manage plant debris responsibly
• Maintain proper spacing, drainage, irrigation, and plant nutrition
• Inspect plants after wet and windy weather, especially older leaves
• Begin management early before lesions merge and reduce functional leaf area
